tour.title: Packaging and CLI Assembly
tour.description: Squadron ships as the `squadron-ai` package and presents itself as one thing: the `sq` command. The pyproject manifest declares the console entry point that binds `sq` to `squadron.cli.app:app`, along with the runtime dependencies that hint at the whole architecture — Typer for the CLI, Pydantic for schemas, FastAPI for the server surface, and four separate LLM SDKs. That entry point lands in `cli/app.py`, a Typer application root that registers every sub-command and has the highest fan-out in the codebase (22 outgoing edges), making it the single best map of what Squadron can do.
tour.languageLesson: Python packaging exposes executables through `[project.scripts]` entry points: a `name = "module.path:callable"` line makes pip/pipx generate a launcher script. Typer builds CLIs from type-annotated function signatures — the annotations become the argument parser, so there is no separate argparse wiring to keep in sync.

tour.title: The `sq review` Command
tour.description: This is the README's headline promise made concrete. `cli/commands/review.py` implements the `sq review` group — `slice`, `arch`, `tasks`, `code`, `list`, and `resolve` — and it is the fourth-highest fan-out file in the project because a single review pulls in templates, models, rules, and git diff inputs before it can run. Read it as the orchestration script for one review: resolve what to review, decide which template applies, execute, render the verdict to the terminal, and persist the result as markdown.

tour.title: Executing a Review
tour.description: Where Step 2 decided what to review, `review_client.py` actually runs it. It builds the final prompt, injects file contents and git diffs, and routes the call through the provider registry's Agent interface — deliberately provider-agnostic, so the same review runs against Anthropic, OpenAI, or the Claude Agent SDK without changing this file. Two supporting modules do the unglamorous work that makes reviews reproducible: `git_utils.py` resolves what "the diff for slice 120" means (locating branches, computing fork points, honoring the configured integration branch), and `rules.py` discovers the project's rules files and folds the relevant ones into the prompt.

tour.title: Templates: Reviews as Data
tour.description: The central design decision of the project: a review type is a YAML file, not a code path. `review/templates/__init__.py` defines the ReviewTemplate dataclass, the YAML loader, and the in-process registry that discovers templates from both built-in and user directories. The shipped `slice.yaml` and `tasks.yaml` are pure declarations — system prompt, tool grant, model, and an inline prompt template. `code.yaml` shows the escape hatch: when a prompt needs real logic, the template names a dotted Python path (`squadron.review.builders.code.code_review_prompt`) and the loader resolves it, letting `builders/code.py` branch between diff-scoped, glob-scoped, and unscoped survey modes.
tour.languageLesson: Dotted-path resolution (importing a module by string name and pulling an attribute off it) is how Python systems stay declarative without losing extensibility. The YAML stays data; the optional hook stays code. Note the discipline in `template_inputs.py` too — instead of a per-template if/elif chain, it declares which input keys each template needs, so adding a template means adding a registry row, not editing a dispatch.

tour.title: Parsing the Verdict
tour.description: An LLM returns markdown; Squadron promises a structured verdict. `parsers.py` bridges the gap, extracting the verdict, score, criteria, and findings out of raw agent output — and crucially, validating that each finding's claimed file location actually exists in the diff or working tree, so a hallucinated line reference does not survive into the result. `models.py` is the vocabulary those parsers produce: the verdict and severity enums, structured and prose findings, and the ReviewResult aggregate. With 15 incoming edges it is one of the most depended-upon types in the codebase. `persistence.py` then writes the result as frontmatter-stamped markdown, archiving prior revisions rather than overwriting them.
tour.languageLesson: Parse leniently, model strictly. The parser anchors on semantic shape rather than exact formatting (whitespace counts, line positions) because a regex that silently drops valid model output is a bug that produces an empty-but-successful review. The enums on the other side give the rest of the system exhaustive, typo-proof comparisons.

tour.title: Did the Findings Get Fixed?
tour.description: A verdict is only half the loop — the other half is proving the findings were actually addressed. The `review/addressed/` package is the shared vocabulary for that question: finding statuses, the readers that lift findings out of a review result, the judge transport, and the parsing and verification layers. The important architectural move lives in `verification.py`: the judge's per-finding claims are checked against the real diff and downgraded to "disputed" when unsupported, so the verdict derives from evidence rather than from the model's own assertion. `screens.py` settles what it can deterministically — a byte-identical round needs no model call at all.

tour.title: Pipelines: Reviews Become Workflows
tour.description: Here the tour widens. Everything so far ran one review; pipelines run many steps in sequence, and they are declared in YAML exactly the way templates are. `loader.py` finds pipeline definitions across built-in, user, and project directories; `schema.py` validates the raw YAML through Pydantic and lowers it into plain dataclasses; `models.py` defines those dataclasses — StepConfig, ActionContext, ActionResult, PipelineDefinition — and with 36 incoming edges it is the second-most depended-upon module in the project. `review.yaml` is the smallest real example: one step that runs a `code` review and pauses for a human when the verdict is CONCERNS or worse.
tour.languageLesson: Note the two-layer type split: Pydantic models validate untrusted YAML at the boundary, then convert into plain `@dataclass` DTOs for internal use. Validation stays at the edge where bad input arrives, and the hot inner loop passes cheap, immutable structures around instead of re-validating on every hop.

tour.title: The Execution Engine
tour.description: `executor.py` is the hub the whole orchestration layer turns around: it merges parameters, resolves placeholders, and walks a PipelineDefinition step by step, handling retry loops, `each`/`fan_out` collection steps, checkpoint pauses, and lazy SDK session connection. `state.py` is what makes those pauses survivable — it persists RunState, StepState, and CheckpointState as JSON with atomic write-then-rename, so a run that stops at a human checkpoint can be resumed later. `prompt_renderer.py` and `resolver.py` handle the substitution and model-resolution cascade the executor leans on for every step.
tour.languageLesson: Atomic write-then-rename is the standard way to persist state safely: write to a temp file, fsync, then `os.replace` onto the target. POSIX rename is atomic, so a crash mid-write leaves either the old file or the new one — never a truncated hybrid that a resume would choke on.

tour.title: Extensibility: Steps and Actions
tour.description: Rather than a switch statement over step kinds, Squadron uses two parallel Protocol-plus-registry pairs. `steps/protocol.py` declares what a step type must do (expand a StepConfig into action pairs, validate its config) and `steps/__init__.py` hosts the registry that bootstraps every built-in implementation. `actions/protocol.py` and `actions/__init__.py` mirror that for actions — the units that actually do work, like `review.py` (which invokes everything from Steps 2-5) and `checkpoint.py` (19 incoming edges, the pause-for-human primitive). Adding a new step or action means writing a class and registering it, never editing the executor.
tour.languageLesson: Python's `typing.Protocol` gives you structural typing — an implementation satisfies the contract by having the right methods, with no base class to inherit from. Marked `@runtime_checkable`, it also supports `isinstance` checks at registration time. This is the Open/Closed Principle in practice: new variants extend the registry instead of modifying a dispatch.

tour.title: The Findings-Addressed Gate
tour.description: This step shows Steps 6 and 9 composing into a real feature. `actions/findings_addressed/policy.py` is a gate policy that sequences zero-cost deterministic screens before the paid judge leg, then derives the verdict from per-finding statuses rather than from what the model declared. `screens.py` adds the loop-specific checks (no prior round; the reviewer re-found it), `judge.py` resolves the judge model through the ActionContext cascade and delegates to the shared review transport from Step 6, and `evidence.py` persists the decision — pointedly named outside the `*-review.*` namespace so metrology never mistakes it for a calibration sample. The `findings-addressed-cycle.yaml` pipeline is what a user actually runs.

tour.title: The Provider Abstraction
tour.description: Every LLM call in Steps 3, 8, and 10 goes through this layer. `providers/base.py` (16 incoming edges) declares the Agent and AgentProvider Protocols plus the capability descriptor and provider/profile/auth enums — no base classes, no inheritance. `registry.py` maps provider type names to instances and `loader.py` imports a provider package lazily, so its module-level auto-registration only runs when that provider is actually needed and unused SDKs never get imported. The Claude Agent SDK provider is the reference implementation: a package barrel that self-registers, a provider factory, an agent with rate-limit retry, and a `translation.py` that converts SDK message types into Squadron's own Message model.
tour.languageLesson: Lazy registration solves a real Python problem: registries populate as a side effect of import, so a naive design must import every provider at startup — dragging in four vendor SDKs to make one call. Importing the package only on demand keeps startup fast and makes an uninstalled optional dependency a runtime error in one provider rather than a crash at process launch.

tour.title: Events and Side Effects
tour.description: Pipelines need hooks — verify an artifact was written, stamp a revision number, block a commit on invalid frontmatter — without those concerns leaking into the executor. `events/__init__.py` defines the closed EventType enum and the module-level registry; `protocol.py` declares the EventAction contract; `dispatcher.py` is the single execution path, running each bound action under a timeout with deliberately different reduction semantics per event kind (collect all failures for COMMIT, stop at the first for POST_ACTION). `manifest.py` resolves `events.yaml` from project then user locations with first-found-wins, and `discovery.py` imports declared plugin modules only — never filesystem scanning.

tour.title: Metrology: Measuring the Runs
tour.description: If reviews are supposed to be repeatable, something has to measure whether they are. The metrology subsystem records and analyzes token, cost, and preemption metrics across runs. `store.py` is an append-only JSON record store with atomic writes and schema-version enforcement, exposing typed readers for samples, graduations, audit runs, and noise floors. `audit.py` drives an end-to-end audit oracle run — resolving the audit skill and profile, preflighting the target repo, dispatching the agent, and recording the findings — while `calibration.py` and `graduation.py` turn accumulated samples into judgments about whether a configuration is trustworthy.

tour.title: Shared Foundation
tour.description: Two modules sit underneath everything you have seen. `logging.py` has 70 incoming edges — nearly a third of the graph — providing one single-line JSON formatter and the shared logger factory, which is why every subsystem's failures come out in a uniform, greppable shape. `config/manager.py` merges user-level and project-level TOML with declared defaults and reads, writes, and unsets typed values; `config/keys.py` handles credentials. `.env.example` documents the ten `ORCH_`-prefixed runtime settings, and `models.toml`/`pools.toml` are the registries that let a pipeline say "use the opus pool" instead of hard-coding a model id.
tour.languageLesson: Centralizing model identifiers in `models.toml` rather than scattering them through code is the anti-magic-value rule at work: a value used in conditionals, lookups, or defaults gets defined once and referenced everywhere, so swapping a model is a one-line config edit rather than a grep-and-pray across the codebase.

tour.title: The Daemon Surface
tour.description: Squadron closes with a second way in. `server/app.py` is a FastAPI application factory wiring the agent and health routers and attaching the SquadronEngine to app state; `engine.py` coordinates between routes and the agent registry from Step 11, owning spawn/shutdown and per-agent conversation history. `daemon.py` handles the process lifecycle — PID file, uvicorn on a Unix socket or port, signal handlers, cleanup. On the other side, `client/http.py` is what the CLI uses to talk to that daemon over the socket, falling back to localhost TCP when no socket exists, and `sq serve` is the command that starts it all.
tour.languageLesson: A Unix domain socket with TCP fallback is a deliberate trade: the socket is faster and is protected by filesystem permissions rather than being reachable from the network, so a local daemon is not accidentally exposed. The TCP path exists for environments where the socket cannot be created — and the fallback is explicit and observable, not silent.
